HR Analytics: Predicting Job Change of Data Scientists¶

Group 9

Business context: Human Resources & employee retention

A company that works in Big Data and Data Science runs training courses and wants to hire data scientists from among the people who complete them. Many candidates sign up, and the company wants to know which of them are looking for a new job and which plan to stay with their current employer. Knowing this helps HR:

  • spend recruiter time on the candidates who are most likely to move,
  • cut the cost and time of the hiring process,
  • plan course content and outreach campaigns.

Goal: build a classification model that predicts target (1 = looking for a job change, 0 = not looking) from a candidate's education, experience, current employer and city.

Workflow in this notebook

  1. Setup
  2. Load the data
  3. Data dictionary
  4. Data quality checks
  5. Target distribution
  6. Exploratory data analysis
  7. Feature engineering
  8. Train / test split
  9. Preprocessing pipeline (categorical encoding)
  10. Model comparison with cross-validation
  11. Hyperparameter tuning
  12. Test-set evaluation
  13. What drives the predictions?
  14. Scoring the unlabelled file aug_test.csv
  15. Saving the model
  16. Conclusions and recommendations

1. Setup¶

What: import the libraries, fix a random seed and set one plotting style for every chart.

Why: a fixed RANDOM_STATE makes the split, cross-validation and models give the same results every time the notebook is re-run. One shared colour pair (blue = not looking, orange = looking for a job change) keeps the charts consistent.

3. Data dictionary¶

Column Type Description
enrollee_id ID Unique ID of the candidate. Used only as an identifier, not as a feature.
city Nominal (123 codes) Code of the city the candidate lives in (e.g. city_103).
city_development_index Numeric, 0.45 to 0.95 Development index of the city, scaled from 0 to 1. Higher means more developed.
gender Nominal Male, Female, Other.
relevent_experience Binary Whether the candidate has experience relevant to data science (spelling as in the source).
enrolled_university Nominal Type of university course the candidate is enrolled in: no_enrollment, Full time course, Part time course.
education_level Ordinal Highest education: Primary School < High School < Graduate < Masters < Phd.
major_discipline Nominal Field of study: STEM, Humanities, Business Degree, Arts, Other, No Major.
experience Ordinal (text) Total work experience in years: <1, 1 to 20, >20.
company_size Ordinal (text) Number of employees at the current employer: <10, 10/49, 50-99, 100-500, 500-999, 1000-4999, 5000-9999, 10000+.
company_type Nominal Type of the current employer: Pvt Ltd, Funded Startup, Early Stage Startup, Public Sector, NGO, Other.
last_new_job Ordinal (text) Years between the previous job and the current job: never, 1, 2, 3, 4, >4.
training_hours Numeric, 1 to 336 Number of training hours the candidate has completed.
target Binary label 0 = not looking for a job change, 1 = looking for a job change.

The same dictionary is saved as Group9_HRJobChange_DataDictionary.md next to this notebook. The table below checks it against the actual data: the type pandas reads, the number of distinct values, the share missing and a few example values.

Before choosing how to fill missing values, we compare the job-change rate of rows where a value is missing with rows where it is present.

In [6]:
rows = []
for col in missing.index:
    is_missing = train[col].isna()
    rows.append({
        "column": col,
        "job_change_rate_when_missing": train.loc[is_missing, "target"].mean(),
        "job_change_rate_when_present": train.loc[~is_missing, "target"].mean(),
    })
missing_vs_target = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("column")
missing_vs_target["difference_pts"] = (
    missing_vs_target["job_change_rate_when_missing"] - missing_vs_target["job_change_rate_when_present"]
) * 100
missing_vs_target.sort_values("difference_pts", ascending=False)

column

company_type 0.3883 0.1838 20.4451
last_new_job 0.3641 0.2468 11.7309
experience 0.3538 0.2490 10.4854

Decision:

  • There are no duplicate rows or IDs, and the two files share no candidates. 49 rows (0.26%) match another row in every column except the ID. Because most columns are coarse categories, two different candidates can easily share a profile, so we keep them.
  • Four columns have a lot of missing data: company_type (~32%), company_size (~31%), gender (~24%) and major_discipline (~15%).
  • Missing values are not random. Candidates with no company_size or company_type are looking for a job about 40% of the time, compared with about 18% when the value is present. Many of them probably have no current employer.
  • So we keep these rows. Dropping them would lose about half the data along with a useful signal. Missing categories are filled with an explicit "Unknown" level, and the few missing numeric values are filled with the median. The filling happens inside the model pipeline (Step 9), so it is learned from the training data only.

5. Target distribution¶

What: check how many candidates fall into each class.

Why: if the classes are imbalanced, accuracy is misleading and we need stratified splits and class weighting.

In [7]:
target_counts = train["target"].astype(int).value_counts().sort_index()
target_share = target_counts / target_counts.sum()
display(pd.DataFrame({"count": target_counts, "share": target_share}).rename(index=CLASS_NAMES))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
bars = ax.bar([CLASS_NAMES[i] for i in target_counts.index], target_counts.values,
              color=[CLASS_COLORS[i] for i in target_counts.index], width=0.55)
for bar, n, s in zip(bars, target_counts.values, target_share.values):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, n + 200, f"{n:,} ({s:.0%})",
            ha="center", color=INK, fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("Candidates")
ax.set_ylim(0, target_counts.max() * 1.15)
ax.set_title("Target distribution")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
count share
target
Not looking (0) 14381 0.7507
Looking for job change (1) 4777 0.2493

Observation: only about 25% of candidates are looking for a job change, so the classes are imbalanced (3 to 1). A model that always predicts "not looking" would be 75% accurate and still find no one. So we:

  • use a stratified train/test split and stratified cross-validation,
  • use class_weight="balanced" where the model supports it,
  • compare models on ROC-AUC (how well they rank candidates) and F1 (the balance of precision and recall for class 1), not accuracy.

Candidates who want to move are much more often in less developed cities: their median index is 0.74, compared with 0.91 for those staying, with a large peak at 0.62. Three quarters of the candidates who stay live in cities with an index above 0.80. It is likely to be the strongest single feature.
  • training_hours looks almost the same for both classes (heavily right-skewed, median around 47 h). On its own it tells us little.

6.2 Categorical features¶

What: for each categorical column, plot the job-change rate per category (missing shown as Unknown), with the overall rate as a dashed reference line.

Why: rates are easier to compare than raw counts across categories of very different sizes. The number of candidates n is shown so that small groups are not over-interpreted.

In [9]:
overall_rate = train["target"].mean()

category_orders = {
    "education_level": ["Primary School", "High School", "Graduate", "Masters", "Phd", "Unknown"],
    "company_size": ["<10", "10/49", "50-99", "100-500", "500-999", "1000-4999", "5000-9999", "10000+", "Unknown"],
    "last_new_job": ["never", "1", "2", "3", "4", ">4", "Unknown"],
}
cat_cols = ["relevent_experience", "enrolled_university", "education_level", "major_discipline",
            "company_size", "company_type", "last_new_job", "gender"]

def rate_table(col):
    s = train[col].fillna("Unknown")
    t = train.groupby(s)["target"].agg(rate="mean", n="count")
    return t.reindex(category_orders.get(col, t.sort_values("rate", ascending=False).index)).dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(12, 15))
for ax, col in zip(axes.ravel(), cat_cols):
    t = rate_table(col)
    colors = [ORANGE if r > overall_rate else BLUE for r in t["rate"]]
    ax.barh(t.index.astype(str), t["rate"], color=colors, height=0.6)
    ax.axvline(overall_rate, color=GREY, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    for y, (r, n) in enumerate(zip(t["rate"], t["n"])):
        ax.text(r + 0.005, y, f"{r:.0%}  (n={int(n):,})", va="center", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
    ax.invert_yaxis()
    ax.set_xlim(0, max(t["rate"].max() * 1.45, 0.5))
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
    ax.set_title(col)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
fig.suptitle(f"Job-change rate by category (dashed line = overall rate {overall_rate:.1%}; "
             "orange = above overall)", y=1.0, fontsize=12, color=INK)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations:

  • Unknown in company_size and company_type has the highest rates (about 40%). As Step 4 showed, missing employer information is a signal on its own.
  • Candidates in a full-time course move more often (38%) than those not enrolled (21%).
  • Candidates without relevant experience have a higher rate (34%) than those with it (21%).
  • Graduates are the most likely to move (28%). Candidates with a Phd or only primary schooling are the least likely.
  • gender shows only small differences outside the Unknown group. We keep it for now and check in Step 13 how much the model uses it (see the fairness note in Step 16).

Observations:

  • city has 123 levels and is very concentrated: city_103 and city_21 alone hold over a third of the candidates. city_21 has a very low development index and a job-change rate of about 60%.
  • Every city has exactly one development index, so city_development_index is a numeric summary of city. We keep both. The index works for rare cities, and the one-hot city columns pick up city effects the index misses. With handle_unknown="ignore" in the encoder, a city that was not in the training data does not cause an error.

7. Feature engineering¶

What:

  • Drop enrollee_id (an identifier with no predictive meaning) and separate out target.
  • Convert experience (<1, 1 to 20, >20) to a number: <1 becomes 0.5 and >20 becomes 21.
  • Convert last_new_job (never, 1 to 4, >4) to a number: never becomes 0 and >4 becomes 5.

Why: both columns are ordered text. As numbers they keep that order (Step 6.3 showed a steady trend), and we avoid adding 28 sparse dummy columns. Missing values stay missing here and are filled with the median inside the pipeline.

In [13]:
EXPERIENCE_MAP = {"<1": 0.5, **{str(i): i for i in range(1, 21)}, ">20": 21}
LAST_JOB_MAP = {"never": 0, "1": 1, "2": 2, "3": 3, "4": 4, ">4": 5}

def prepare_features(df):
    X = df.drop(columns=["enrollee_id", "target"], errors="ignore").copy()
    X["experience_num"] = X["experience"].map(EXPERIENCE_MAP)
    X["last_new_job_num"] = X["last_new_job"].map(LAST_JOB_MAP)
    return X.drop(columns=["experience", "last_new_job"])

X = prepare_features(train)
y = train["target"].astype(int)

# Check: every non-missing text value was mapped (no new NaNs created)
assert X["experience_num"].isna().sum() == train["experience"].isna().sum()
assert X["last_new_job_num"].isna().sum() == train["last_new_job"].isna().sum()

print("Feature matrix:", X.shape)
X.head()

8. Train / test split¶

What: hold out a stratified 20% of the labelled data as a test set.

Why: aug_test.csv has no labels, so we need our own hold-out set to measure performance. Model selection and tuning (Steps 10 and 11) use only the 80% training part. The test set is used once, in Step 12. Stratifying keeps the 25% job-change rate the same in both parts.

In [14]:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20, random_state=RANDOM_STATE, stratify=y
)
pd.DataFrame({
    "rows": [len(X_train), len(X_test)],

9. Preprocessing pipeline (categorical encoding)¶

What: a ColumnTransformer that treats each type of column differently.

Group Columns Missing values Encoding Why
Nominal city, gender, relevent_experience, enrolled_university, major_discipline, company_type constant "Unknown" One-hot (handle_unknown="ignore") No natural order, so each category gets its own 0/1 column. Unseen categories are ignored instead of causing an error.
Ordinal education_level, company_size constant "Unknown" Ordinal, with an explicit order Categories have a real order (Primary School up to Phd; <10 up to 10000+). Unknown is placed first (code 0).
Numeric city_development_index, training_hours, experience_num, last_new_job_num median Standard scaling Puts features on a comparable scale, which distance-based (KNN) and regularised (logistic regression) models need.

Why a pipeline: the imputers and encoders are fitted inside each cross-validation fold, on training data only. This prevents data leakage, where the validation or test rows would influence preprocessing.

In [15]:
NOMINAL = ["city", "gender", "relevent_experience", "enrolled_university", "major_discipline", "company_type"]
ORDINAL = ["education_level", "company_size"]
NUMERIC = ["city_development_index", "training_hours", "experience_num", "last_new_job_num"]

EDUCATION_ORDER = ["Unknown", "Primary School", "High School", "Graduate", "Masters", "Phd"]
COMPANY_SIZE_ORDER = ["Unknown", "<10", "10/49", "50-99", "100-500", "500-999",
                      "1000-4999", "5000-9999", "10000+"]

def build_preprocessor():
    nominal = Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Unknown")),
        ("onehot", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")),
    ])
    ordinal = Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Unknown")),
        ("ordinal", OrdinalEncoder(categories=[EDUCATION_ORDER, COMPANY_SIZE_ORDER],
                                   handle_unknown="use_encoded_value", unknown_value=-1)),
    ])
    numeric = Pipeline([
        ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ])
    return ColumnTransformer([
        ("nominal", nominal, NOMINAL),
        ("ordinal", ordinal, ORDINAL),
        ("numeric", numeric, NUMERIC),
    ], remainder="drop")

# Fit once on the training data only to inspect the result
preview = build_preprocessor().fit(X_train)
n_out = preview.transform(X_train.head(1)).shape[1]
print(f"{X_train.shape[1]} raw columns become {n_out} model features after encoding")
print("One-hot columns per nominal feature:",
      {c: len(cats) for c, cats in zip(NOMINAL, preview.named_transformers_["nominal"]["onehot"].categories_)})

12 raw columns become 152 model features after encoding
One-hot columns per nominal feature: {'city': 122, 'gender': 4, 'relevent_experience': 2, 'enrolled_university': 4, 'major_discipline': 7, 'company_type': 7}

10. Model comparison with cross-validation¶

What: compare five models with 5-fold stratified cross-validation on the training set:

Model Why it is included
Dummy (always predicts the majority class) Baseline. Any useful model has to beat it.
Logistic Regression Simple, fast and interpretable linear model.
Decision Tree Captures non-linear rules, but tends to overfit.
Random Forest Many trees averaged together. Usually strong on tabular data.
K-Nearest Neighbours Classifies a candidate by looking at the most similar candidates.

Why cross-validation: one split can be lucky or unlucky. Averaging over 5 folds gives a steadier estimate, and the standard deviation shows how much each model varies. Models are ranked by ROC-AUC, with F1 shown alongside.

In [16]:
models = {
    "Dummy": DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"),
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, class_weight="balanced",
                                            random_state=RANDOM_STATE, n_jobs=-1),
    "KNN": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15),
}

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
pipelines, rows = {}, []
for name, estimator in models.items():
    pipe = Pipeline([("preprocessor", build_preprocessor()), ("model", estimator)])
    pipelines[name] = pipe
    scores = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring={"f1": "f1", "roc_auc": "roc_auc"}, n_jobs=-1)
    rows.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Mean_ROC_AUC": scores["test_roc_auc"].mean(), "Std_ROC_AUC": scores["test_roc_auc"].std(),
        "Mean_F1": scores["test_f1"].mean(), "Std_F1": scores["test_f1"].std(),
    })

cv_results = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("Mean_ROC_AUC", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
cv_results

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.4), sharey=True)
order = cv_results["Model"][::-1]
for ax, metric in zip(axes, ["ROC_AUC", "F1"]):
    r = cv_results.set_index("Model").loc[order]
    ax.barh(r.index, r[f"Mean_{metric}"], xerr=r[f"Std_{metric}"], color=BLUE, height=0.55,
            error_kw={"ecolor": INK, "capsize": 3, "linewidth": 1})
    for yy, v in enumerate(r[f"Mean_{metric}"]):
        ax.text(v + 0.02, yy, f"{v:.3f}", va="center", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
    ax.set_title(f"Cross-validated {metric.replace('_', '-')} (mean ± std, 5 folds)")
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

best_name = cv_results.loc[0, "Model"]
assert best_name != "Dummy", "Dummy baseline ranked first; review the modelling setup."
print("Best model by cross-validated ROC-AUC:", best_name)

Best model by cross-validated ROC-AUC: Logistic Regression

Observations:

  • Every model beats the Dummy baseline (ROC-AUC 0.50, F1 0.00), so the features do help predict the target.
  • Logistic Regression, KNN and Random Forest are close (ROC-AUC between 0.78 and 0.79). The differences are about the size of one standard deviation. Logistic Regression ranks first and also has the best F1.
  • The unpruned Decision Tree is clearly the weakest (about 0.62), most likely because it overfits the training folds.
  • When models score about the same, we prefer the simpler one. Logistic Regression can be explained through its coefficients, which is useful when HR needs to understand a prediction.

11. Hyperparameter tuning¶

What: tune the best model from Step 10 with GridSearchCV, using the same 5 folds and refitting on ROC-AUC. A grid is defined for every candidate model, so the notebook still works if a different model comes out on top.

For Logistic Regression we tune the regularisation strength C (smaller means a simpler model) and the penalty type (l1 can set weak features to zero, l2 shrinks all of them).

In [18]:
grids = {
    "Logistic Regression": {"model__C": [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10], "model__solver": ["liblinear"],
                            "model__penalty": ["l1", "l2"]},
    "Decision Tree": {"model__max_depth": [4, 6, 8, 12, None], "model__min_samples_split": [2, 10, 30],
                      "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 15]},
    "Random Forest": {"model__n_estimators": [200, 400], "model__max_depth": [6, 10, None],
                      "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10], "model__max_features": ["sqrt", 0.5]},
    "KNN": {"model__n_neighbors": [7, 15, 25, 35], "model__weights": ["uniform", "distance"], "model__p": [1, 2]},
}

search = GridSearchCV(pipelines[best_name], grids[best_name], scoring={"f1": "f1", "roc_auc": "roc_auc"},
                      refit="roc_auc", cv=cv, n_jobs=-1)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
final_model = search.best_estimator_

print("Best parameters:", search.best_params_)
print(f"Best cross-validated ROC-AUC: {search.best_score_:.4f} "
      f"(untuned: {cv_results.loc[0, 'Mean_ROC_AUC']:.4f})")

param_cols = [f"param_{p}" for p in grids[best_name]]
(pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_)[param_cols + ["mean_test_roc_auc", "std_test_roc_auc", "mean_test_f1"]]
   .sort_values("mean_test_roc_auc", ascending=False).head(8).reset_index(drop=True))

12. Test-set evaluation¶

What: score the tuned model once on the 20% hold-out set it has never seen, and compare it with the Dummy baseline at the default 0.5 threshold.

In [19]:

        "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
        "Recall": recall_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
        "F1": f1_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
        "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_true, prob),
    }

test_metrics = pd.DataFrame({

Observations:

  • On unseen data the tuned model reaches a ROC-AUC of 0.81, close to the cross-validation estimate (0.79), so there is no sign of overfitting.
  • Because of class_weight="balanced" the model leans towards recall. It finds 78% of the candidates who are looking to move, at a precision of 52%, so about one in two flagged candidates is a real job-seeker.
  • The Dummy model's accuracy (75%) is close to the tuned model's (77%), but it finds no job-seekers at all. This is why accuracy was not used to choose the model.

12.1 Choosing a decision threshold¶

What: the model outputs a probability, and 0.5 is only the default cut-off. The table shows how precision, recall and the share of candidates flagged change with the threshold.

Why: the right threshold depends on the business. If recruiter time is scarce, raise it (fewer but more certain flags). If missing a job-seeker is costly, lower it.

Note: in a real project the threshold would be chosen on validation data. It is shown on the test set here only to illustrate the trade-off, not to tune it.

In [22]:
threshold_rows = []
for t in [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8]:
    p = (y_prob >= t).astype(int)
    threshold_rows.append({
        "threshold": t,
        "share_flagged": p.mean(),
        "precision": precision_score(y_test, p, zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(y_test, p, zero_division=0),
        "f1": f1_score(y_test, p, zero_division=0),
    })
pd.DataFrame(threshold_rows).set_index("threshold")

13. What drives the predictions?¶

13.1 Permutation importance (per original column)¶

What: shuffle one original column at a time in the test set and measure how much ROC-AUC drops. A bigger drop means the model relies on that column more.

Why: this works for any model and scores each original column as a whole (for example all the one-hot city columns together), which is easier to explain than single dummy columns.

In [23]:

13.2 Logistic regression coefficients¶

What: the largest positive and negative coefficients of the final model, in terms of the encoded features.

How to read them: a positive coefficient raises the predicted chance of a job change and a negative one lowers it. For one-hot features the effect is relative to the other categories of the same column. Numeric features are standardised, so their coefficients are per one standard deviation.

In [24]:
if isinstance(final_model.named_steps["model"], LogisticRegression):
    feature_names = final_model.named_steps["preprocessor"].get_feature_names_out()
    coefs = pd.Series(final_model.named_steps["model"].coef_[0], index=feature_names)
    coefs.index = (coefs.index.str.replace(r"^(nominal|ordinal|numeric)__", "", regex=True)
                   .str.replace("city_city_", "city_", regex=False))
    top = pd.concat([coefs.nlargest(10), coefs.nsmallest(10)]).sort_values()

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    ax.barh(top.index, top.values, color=[ORANGE if v > 0 else BLUE for v in top.values], height=0.65)
    ax.axvline(0, color=GREY, linewidth=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("Coefficient (log-odds)")
    ax.set_title("Top 10 features raising (orange) and lowering (blue) the job-change probability")
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
else:
    print(f"Coefficient view is only available for Logistic Regression (selected: {best_name}).")

Observations:

  • city_development_index is the most important feature. Shuffling it lowers ROC-AUC by about 0.10, twice as much as any other column, and its coefficient is strongly negative: candidates from less developed cities are much more likely to be looking to move.
  • company_type and city come next, followed by major_discipline and company_size.
    • company_type = Unknown (no current-employer information) is one of the strongest positive coefficients, while working at a Funded Startup strongly lowers the probability.
    • Many of the largest coefficients belong to individual cities, for example city_21 (the large low-development city from Step 6.4). These columns add city effects on top of the development index.
    • major_discipline = Unknown has the largest negative coefficient. Candidates with no recorded major have a low job-change rate (about 20%, Step 4), which is why this column ranks fourth in importance.
  • More experience and having relevant experience have smaller negative coefficients: more senior candidates with relevant experience tend to stay.
  • training_hours, gender and last_new_job add almost nothing. The model barely uses gender.

16. Conclusions and recommendations¶

In [27]:
summary = test_metrics[f"Tuned {best_name}"]
print(f"Final model      : {best_name} {search.best_params_}")
print(f"Test ROC-AUC     : {summary['ROC-AUC']:.3f}")
print(f"Test F1          : {summary['F1']:.3f}")
print(f"Test recall      : {summary['Recall']:.3f}  (share of real job-seekers found)")
print(f"Test precision   : {summary['Precision']:.3f}  (share of flagged candidates who are real job-seekers)")

Final model      : Logistic Regression {'model__C': 0.1, 'model__penalty': 'l2', 'model__solver': 'liblinear'}
Test ROC-AUC     : 0.808
Test F1          : 0.628
Test recall      : 0.783  (share of real job-seekers found)
Test precision   : 0.524  (share of flagged candidates who are real job-seekers)
Top 3 drivers    : city_development_index, company_type, city

Summary

  • A tuned Logistic Regression predicts whether a candidate is looking for a job change with a ROC-AUC of 0.81 on unseen data, against 0.50 for the baseline. It finds 78% of real job-seekers, and about half of the candidates it flags are real job-seekers.
  • Logistic Regression scored as well as or better than Random Forest and KNN, and it is easier to explain to HR.
  • Encoding: one-hot for nominal columns (including the 123-level city), ordinal encoding for ordered categories, numbers for experience and last_new_job, and an explicit Unknown level, because a missing value is itself related to job change.

What drives job change

  1. City development: candidates from less developed cities are much more likely to want to move. This is the strongest signal.
  2. Current employer: candidates with no recorded company size or type (probably often not employed) are the most likely to move.
  3. Career stage: candidates with under 2 years of experience, candidates without relevant experience and full-time students move most often.
  4. Training hours: these make almost no difference to whether someone wants to move.

Recommendations for HR

  • Use the predicted probability to rank candidates and start recruiter outreach at the top of the list, rather than treating it as a yes/no rule.
  • Choose the threshold according to recruiter capacity (Step 12.1): about 0.5 to find most job-seekers, about 0.7 for a shorter and more precise list.
  • Aim recruiting campaigns at training groups from less developed cities and at early-career candidates.

Limitations

  • About 1 in 2 flagged candidates is a false positive, so a recruiter should still review each case.
  • gender is a sensitive attribute. It has the lowest permutation importance of all columns (about 0.0006 ROC-AUC). We checked: retraining without it changes test ROC-AUC only from 0.8085 to 0.8082. It should be removed before the model is used for real decisions.
  • city and city_development_index may stand in for socio-economic background. The model should be checked for fairness before it is used.
  • The data comes from one training programme at one point in time, so the model should be checked again on newer data before use.

Deployment Extension — CatBoost Ensemble¶

The course-model comparison above remains the academic benchmark. For the website deployment, we added a three-seed CatBoost ensemble as an advanced extension because the data contains many categorical variables, substantial missingness, and non-linear interactions. This extension was evaluated on a fresh locked 20% stratified test split (random_state=2026). Model selection and decision-threshold selection used only the 80% development partition through 5-fold out-of-fold predictions. The locked test set was opened only for final evaluation.

This section is intentionally reported separately from the historical notebook split, so metrics from different splits are not compared as if they were identical experiments.

In [ ]:
# Final deployment-model results, loaded from the frozen experiment artifacts
from pathlib import Path
import json
import pandas as pd

_candidates = [Path('../model'), Path('model'), Path.cwd().parent / 'model']
model_dir = next((p.resolve() for p in _candidates if (p / 'final_test_metrics.json').exists()), None)
if model_dir is None:
    raise FileNotFoundError('Could not locate model/final_test_metrics.json. Run this notebook from the presentation package.')

with open(model_dir / 'final_test_metrics.json', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    enhanced = json.load(f)
with open(model_dir / 'baseline_locked_split.json', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    baseline = json.load(f)

rows = [
    {
        'Model': 'Original Logistic Regression (OOF accuracy threshold)',
        'Threshold': baseline['oof_accuracy_threshold'],
        'Accuracy': baseline['test_at_tuned_accuracy_threshold']['accuracy'],
        'Precision': baseline['test_at_tuned_accuracy_threshold']['precision'],
        'Recall': baseline['test_at_tuned_accuracy_threshold']['recall'],
        'F1': baseline['test_at_tuned_accuracy_threshold']['f1'],
        'ROC-AUC': baseline['test_at_tuned_accuracy_threshold']['roc_auc'],
    },
    {
        'Model': 'CatBoost ensemble (default deployment)',
        'Threshold': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['threshold'],
        'Accuracy': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['accuracy'],
        'Precision': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['precision'],
        'Recall': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['recall'],
        'F1': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['f1'],
        'ROC-AUC': enhanced['test_at_accuracy_threshold']['roc_auc'],
    },
]
comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows)
comparison.style.format({
    'Threshold':'{:.3f}', 'Accuracy':'{:.4f}', 'Precision':'{:.4f}',
    'Recall':'{:.4f}', 'F1':'{:.4f}', 'ROC-AUC':'{:.4f}'
})

Deployment conclusion¶

On the same locked split, the CatBoost deployment ensemble improves ROC-AUC from 0.7923 to 0.8036. At each model's validation-selected accuracy threshold, accuracy changes from 79.12% to 80.19% and F1 from 0.5914 to 0.6307. The gain is useful but incremental rather than transformational; the next major improvement is more likely to come from richer longitudinal/behavioural data and external validation than from increasingly complex tuning on the same dataset.

The website uses the three saved CatBoost models through a FastAPI endpoint and averages their predictions for live inference.
